# Conceptual foundations

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What fitting means

Choose the parameters $\theta = (\beta, \gamma)$ so that the model's output is [as close as possible]{style="color: tomato;"} to the data $\mathbf{y}$

- Everything depends on what we mean by *close*
- Whatever we decide, we write it as a number: an [objective function]{style="color: tomato;"} $\mathcal{L}(\theta, \mathbf{y})$ that is small when the curve is near the data and large when it is far away
- Fitting then means searching over $\theta$ for the values that make that number small

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Two ways to answer

### A point estimate

$$\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta, \mathbf{y})$$

The next two sections use two different choices of $\mathcal{L}$, the sum of squared errors and then the negative log-likelihood

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### A distribution

A probability for *every* $\theta$ given the data, rather than the one best value

$$p(\theta \mid \mathbf{y})$$

This is Bayesian inference, and it is where the lecture ends up. The two answers share the likelihood, which we build in section 4

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why the model will never match the data exactly {.smaller}

Even with the right $\beta$ and $\gamma$ the curve will not pass through every point. There are several reasons for the mismatch, and the lecture deals with each of them somewhere

| Source | In the flu data | Where we deal with it |
|---|---|---|
| Observation | Not every pupil in bed was infectious, or counted | The likelihood (4) |
| Parameter | Several $(\beta, \gamma)$ pairs fit almost as well | Confidence intervals (4), the posterior (6) |
| Model | No latent period; everyone mixes with everyone | Model comparison (4) |
| Process | Chance in who infected whom, day by day | Particle filtering (7) |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Identifiability {.smaller}

[**The problem:**]{style="color: tomato;"} different parameter combinations can produce nearly the same curve

- A high $\beta$ with a high $\gamma$: fast spread, quick recovery
- A low $\beta$ with a low $\gamma$: slow spread, long infections
- Both can give a similar epidemic, because what the data pin down is mostly the ratio $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$

We will meet this three times today: as a tilted valley in the least squares surface, as wide profile likelihoods, and as a tilted cloud of posterior samples

[**The way out:**]{style="color: tomato;"} bring in what you already know, for instance a plausible infectious period for influenza. In the Bayesian section that is exactly what a prior is

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where to start

We start with the simplest objective function there is, the sum of squared distances between the points and the curve
